doc.title: Ray Vega interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 20, 2023

title: Doing any work for a living: Golijov tours, weddings, salsa and church gigs
summary: Vega describes touring with Osvaldo Golijov, weddings, salsa and church jobs, and how he succeeded in salsa bands by being prepared; Mongo Santamaria gave him a chance in 1987.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: Day jobs: musicians working outside music

blocks.x: No. You’ve got to go in there and get — so I was doing that, I was doing contemporary classical music — like I traveled around the world with — one of the last projects I did was with Osvaldo Golijov. He’s a conductor of contemporary classical music from Argentina. He’s a composer rather, of contemporary classical music from Argentina. We traveled all over the world. And I wasn’t playing bebop on that. I was playing C trumpet, piccolo trumpet and B flat trumpet in this work that he had. Right? Again was I playing “spang-a-lang”? No. But guess what. I was doing what I needed to do because I had a wife and three kids and mortgage payments and needed to get paid. And I wasn’t going to sit there going, “Man you know I want to play my music.” No, no, no, no, no, no, no. I was not — I did not come up with a trust fund where my parents had some money set aside for me so that I can move to New York and be creative and move to an apartment in the West Village that they’re paying the rent for while I try to discover who I am. No. No, no, no, no, no, no. This was about work. So I did everything from weddings, salsa gigs, big band gigs, dance bands. You’ve got to do whatever you can. I don’t know how many times this is my life: play Sunday — Saturday night with a salsa band but remember you’ve got to be at church at 6:00 in the morning because they’re having © Fillius Jazz Archive -17-

sunrise service and you’ve got to go in there and play “The Trumpet Shall Sound” and Handel’s “Messiah” on D trumpet. Okay, get ready, and you’re going to go there with your puffy salsa chops going in there. And was I doing it because I necessarily wanted it? I was proud of my skill set and I would do it, but my endorphins were not going woo this is awesome. This is about I have to pay my bills. You know? So I often tell my students when I first started to break in like the salsa music scene man I was not the best player by any stretch of the imagination. But what I was was the guy who got there early and asked the band leader, “What time is the gig tomorrow, oh okay.” And I’ll get to the gig early. “What are we wearing?” The black suit. Okay wear the black suit, show up, don’t bug the lead trumpet player with ten thousand questions about how to play the music, sit there, shut up, listen to the lead trumpet player, follow that person from here to eternity, get the job done. Because I needed to work. Did I want to be out there playing other kinds of things? Of course I did. You know? Thank goodness that Mongo Santamaria in 1987 gave me the opportunity to join his band and then that introduced me to a whole world of like jazz clubs and going out for a month and a half in the United States, going to Europe for European tours. So that opened me up to a whole different circle of players and gigs etcetera. But I learned from that. It wasn’t like — oh I’m on Mongo’s band, all I’m going to do is play creative music. No. And also another thing is this, before I started to teach I would always have a side hustle whether it was working at a preschool, working at a middle school, and they would always understand mind you — I’ve got to keep this one quiet here.
